teaser: Five dancers, three colors, and a Paris crowd that laughed out loud.
review_notes:
IMAGE MISMATCH: the image shows Dance (I), 1909, Museum of Modern Art, New York (pale pink figures), not the 1910 Hermitage canvas listed in the metadata (brick-red figures). The lesson says so explicitly and points only at what this image shows. If the image is replaced by the Hermitage version, the paragraph on the two versions and the color descriptions in the spots need rewriting.
Shchukin cancelling and then reversing his decision by telegram from the train: standard account, check wording.
Size of the Hermitage canvas given as 260 x 391 cm.
Sources for the motif (Catalan sardana at Collioure, farandole at the Moulin de la Galette) are Matisse's own later recollections.

lesson.text: October 1910, the Salon d'Automne in Paris. Visitors stop in front of two enormous panels by Henri Matisse, Dance and Music, and many of them laugh. Critics write of cannibals and cavemen. The man who ordered the paintings, the Russian merchant Sergei Shchukin, is in town, hears all of it, and loses his nerve.

Shchukin had asked for decorations for the staircase of his Moscow mansion. Now he worried about naked bodies greeting his guests, in a house where young girls lived. He told Matisse he would not take them. Then, on the long train ride home, he changed his mind and sent word: send the panels.

A note before you look. The image here is the first full-size version, painted quickly in 1909 to show Shchukin the idea, and now kept at the Museum of Modern Art in New York. The final canvas in the Hermitage, dated 1910, has the same five dancers in a fiercer key: brick-red bodies, darker outlines, harder muscles.

Both versions are about 2.6 meters high and 3.9 meters wide, roughly 8.5 by 13 feet. Each dancer is larger than you are. On a staircase, visitors would have climbed toward them, as if joining the circle from below.

Matisse built the whole thing from three colors: blue for sky, green for a hill, one flesh tone for bodies. No trees, no horizon, no faces to speak of. With so little to look at, the only subject left is the movement itself. So how does a still picture spin?
Trace the two shapes that set the ring turning.

lines.label: The ring
lines.text: Linked arms make a lopsided oval, squeezed to fit the frame. It tilts, high on the left and low on the right, like a wheel seen at an angle.

lines.label: The hill
lines.text: The ground is a single mound. It bulges up under the dancers' feet as if their weight and speed were pressing it into shape.

lines.label: The anchor
lines.text: The tall figure on the left stretches almost from the bottom edge to the top. She is the upright post the others whirl around.

lesson.text: The dancers on the left and at the back are fairly upright. On the right they tip over, and the one in front is nearly horizontal, flung outward and scrambling to keep up. Read from left to right, the ring accelerates.
The circle is not closed. Somewhere two hands have lost each other. Tap the gap.

spots.title: The broken link
spots.text: The front dancer stretches out her hand, and the tall one's fingers are just out of reach. Matisse set the gap against a knee so it does not tear a hole in the design.

lesson.text: That small gap carries a lot. A closed ring would be a pattern, complete and at rest. An open one is an event: something has just slipped and must be caught. It also happens to be the point nearest to you, which has led many viewers to feel that the missing hand is theirs.

Matisse said the idea came from dances he had watched: Catalan fishermen circling on the beach at Collioure, and the farandole at the Moulin de la Galette, a Paris dance hall. He recalled humming the dance hall tune while he painted.

lesson.title: Painted at speed
lesson.text: This first version shows its making more openly than the final one.

spots.title: Shifted outlines
spots.text: Around the shoulders and arms you can see pale halos and dark second thoughts where Matisse moved a contour. He corrected by redrawing, not by hiding.

spots.title: A body like a bow
spots.text: The dancer at the right edge arches backward, head thrown out of the ring. Anatomy gives way to one long curve from heel to hair.

spots.title: The faller
spots.text: Seen from behind, hair hanging forward, one leg trailing to the corner. Her back is modeled with a few gray strokes and nothing more.

lesson.text: Dance and Music hung on Shchukin's staircase until the revolution swept his collection into state museums. The laughter of 1910 did not last. Within a few decades this ring of figures had become shorthand for modern art itself, copied on posters, record sleeves and classroom walls.
Dance shows how much a painter can remove. With three colors and five bodies, Matisse gets rhythm, weight and joy, and nothing distracts from them.

quiz.question: How did the public react when Dance was first shown in Paris in 1910?
quiz.explanation: Visitors laughed and critics wrote of cannibals and cavemen.

quiz.question: Where was the painting meant to hang?
options: On the staircase of Shchukin's Moscow mansion
quiz.explanation: Shchukin ordered Dance and Music as staircase decorations.

quiz.question: How many main colors did Matisse use?
quiz.explanation: Blue sky, green hill and one flesh tone.

quiz.question: What is special about the hands of the two dancers at the front left?
options: They are hidden behind the hill
quiz.explanation: The ring is broken there: the hands reach but do not meet.

quiz.question: How does the 1910 Hermitage canvas differ from the 1909 version shown here?
options: Its bodies are brick red with darker outlines
quiz.explanation: The final version keeps the composition in a much fiercer color key.

facts.text: Shchukin first refused the panels, then changed his mind on the train home.
facts.explanation: He cancelled after the Paris scandal and then asked Matisse to send them after all.

facts.text: The dancers are small figures, about the size of a hand.
facts.explanation: The canvas is about 2.6 by 3.9 meters, and each dancer is larger than life.

facts.text: Matisse linked the idea to dances he had seen in Collioure and in a Paris dance hall.
facts.explanation: He mentioned Catalan fishermen and the farandole at the Moulin de la Galette.
